summary: Defines requirements for protocols used by Network Access Servers, the devices that let users connect to a network.

plainLanguage.summary: It lists what a gatekeeper protocol for dial-in doors needs to do.

questions: what is a network access server
what attributes must an aaa protocol support
subtitle: A checklist of what an authentication, authorization and accounting protocol must do for network access servers.

tldr.problem: Network Access Servers (NAS) let users in over dial-up, broadband or tunnels, and need a protocol to ask a central server who may connect, on what terms, and how to bill for it. Existing practice was RADIUS, and a successor needed a clear list of requirements.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists MUST, SHOULD and MAY requirements for a NAS access protocol and, in much more detail, for an AAA protocol: transport, attribute-value data, security, authentication, authorization and accounting.
tldr.outcome: It is a set of evaluation criteria, not a protocol. Any candidate AAA protocol can be measured against it.

facts.label: Access protocol baseline
facts.value: MUST be able to carry PPP

today: RFC 3169 is an Informational RFC from September 2001, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines evaluation criteria rather than a protocol, and builds on the NAS model in RFC 2881.

sections.title: Scope: Four Kinds of NAS Protocol
sections.content:
RFC 3169 defines requirements for the protocols used by Network Access Servers (NAS). It divides them into four spaces: access protocols, network protocols, AAA protocols and device management protocols. The main focus is on AAA (authentication, authorization and accounting) protocols.

The RFC uses the key words MUST, SHOULD and MAY as defined in RFC 2119. The NAS reference model behind the requirements is in RFC 2881.
sections.plainLanguage: A door guard deals with four kinds of rules: how people arrive, what network they get, who checks their papers, and how the guard's own equipment is managed. This list mostly covers the paper-checking part.

sections.title: Access and Network Protocol Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC names three kinds of access protocol. Traditional telephony-based ones reach the NAS through a modem or terminal adapter, and typically carry asynchronous or synchronous PPP. Broadband pseudo-telephony ones run over xDSL or cable modems, typically using an encapsulation such as PPP over Ethernet. Virtual access protocols are used by NAS devices that terminate tunnels, for example L2TP.

The central assumption is that a NAS accepts multiple point-to-point links, so any NAS access protocol MUST be able to carry PPP. Only access protocols for legacy text logins such as telnet, rlogin or LAT are exempt.

The network protocols a NAS supports depend on the network it serves, and the RFC adds no requirements of its own. For example, a NAS that does routing must follow the router requirements already in force.
sections.plainLanguage: However people come in, by phone line, by broadband or through a tunnel, the door must understand the common language for one-to-one links, called PPP.

sections.title: General AAA Protocol Design
sections.content:
The AAA protocol MUST be transport independent. Existing deployments use UDP-based protocols such as RADIUS, and gateways to new protocols should be practical. It must follow congestion control recommendations in RFC 2914. It must scale to a large number of ports, clients and concurrent sessions, avoiding small identifier ranges and counters that wrap too soon.

It must let a NAS balance requests between two or more AAA servers and fail over to a secondary server without losing state, with no single point of failure. It must also work across multiple administrative domains and support proxying, and should support brokering and referral.

Data should be an attribute-value model. The protocol MUST support at least 64K attributes (16 bits), each with a minimum length of 64K (16 bits), basic types (integer, enumeration, text string, IP address, date/time) and both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. It must cover at least the attributes of RADIUS and RADIUS Accounting, allow new attributes to be registered through IANA, and allow vendor-specific attributes.

For security, NAS and server MUST authenticate each other. Shared secrets are the minimum for small deployments, but public-key mutual verification with expiry and revocation MUST also be supported, along with encryption of selected attributes, attribute by attribute, even within one message.
sections.plainLanguage: The checklist says the system must handle huge crowds, keep working if one office phone breaks, work between different companies, and let the guard and the office check each other's identity.

sections.title: Authentication Requirements
sections.content:
The AAA protocol carries the credentials users present between the NAS and the AAA server. It MUST support re-authentication at any time in a session, started by either the NAS or the server, and multi-phase methods such as text prompts, a series of binary challenges and responses, failure reasons sent back to the user, and callback to a fixed phone number. It MUST allow new credential types to be added.

It must act as an intermediary for the PPP authentication protocols PAP, CHAP and EAP. It must carry user names in Network Access Identifier form, EAP identity packets, and telephony data such as DNIS and Caller ID. Credentials it must carry include passwords, challenge responses, one-time passwords, X.509 certificates and Kerberos v5 tickets. Dummy credentials must not be required when none are needed.

Passwords MUST be hidden from intermediaries in the AAA conversation, and challenge/response methods MUST be protected against replay attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: The guard must be able to pass along any kind of proof of who you are, such as a password, a code or a certificate, and ask for it again later. Secret words must stay hidden from anyone passing the message along.

sections.title: Authorization and Resource Management
sections.content:
Authorization data sent by the NAS to the AAA server is only information or hints, never directives: the server makes the final decision. The protocol MUST support dynamic re-authorization at any time, started in either direction, including a request to disconnect a user on demand. Resource management, such as allocating IP addresses or limits on concurrent use, ports and tunnels, must also be possible at any time.

Policy decisions must be possible on time and day, location, dialing information and concurrent login limits. When access is granted, the protocol MUST be able to apply a profile containing:

  • an IPv4 or IPv6 address assignment,
  • protocol filters, either by reference to an identifier or passed by value (address range, TCP/UDP port number, IP protocol number),
  • compulsory tunneling, with multiple tunnels in order, covering at least L2TP, ESP and AH,
  • a static route,
  • expirations for total session time, idle time, bytes sent and bytes received,
  • quality of service parameters.

Tunnel credentials passed this way MUST be protected end-to-end and against replay.
sections.plainLanguage: The guard only suggests things to the office, and the office decides. The office can change its mind mid-visit, even send you home, and it hands out the visitor badge with the rules: address, time limit and speed.

sections.title: Accounting and Auditing Requirements
sections.content:
The AAA protocol MUST give guaranteed delivery of accounting data between the NAS and the AAA servers, and MUST support real-time delivery, defined here as delivery beginning within one second of the triggering event. It SHOULD also support batch delivery of stored records. Every accounting event MUST carry an unambiguous time stamp, including the time zone.

At a minimum, accounting must be triggered by the start and end of a session, a repeating interval (which the server can ask the NAS to use), dynamic re-authorization and dynamic re-authentication. The server must also be able to ask the NAS for current session state on demand.

The data reported must include authentication parameters, the authorization profile applied, session duration, bytes and packets sent and received, and details of the access protocol used. Integrity of accounting data MUST be assured end-to-end, confidentiality SHOULD be, and the protocol SHOULD make it hard for the source to deny the data later. Device management protocols get no requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: The guard must write down when each visit started and ended, how much you used and what rules applied, and send the notes to the office quickly and reliably.

items.title: Access protocols
items.text: How users reach the NAS: telephony, broadband, or tunnels. Must carry PPP.

items.title: Network protocols
items.text: Depend on the network served. No extra requirements.

items.title: AAA protocols
items.text: Authentication, authorization and accounting. The main focus of the RFC.
